title: What is known about 1RB0LF_1RC1RA_0RD0RB_1LE---_0LA1LE_1RD1LA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LF_1RC1RA_0RD0RB_1LE---_0LA1LE_1RD1LA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Reported to halt: an external Rocq proof exists (busycoq pull request 60, by Yeyito, 7 November 2026), which we have not compiled. It proves a map on tapes A(a, b) from the raw machine and checks, with 313 compiled jobs (275 core-hours by its README), that the orbit from blank tape reaches the halting case at a = 28·285 − 6, about 1055 steps. We cross-checked it against our own Lean map: its state (a, b) is our round P((a−6)/2, b), its first 2,000,000 map steps all appear in order in our orbit, and both maps halt from the same final round. The middle of the orbit (about 1025 returns) rests on that proof alone. Until it is compiled here or merged upstream, this page keeps the machine as open.

Our own result: reduced in Lean to a question about an explicit map. It is a Lean theorem (kernel-checked, no native_decide) that the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit of the reset configuration S(13) = 0^inf 1^13 1110 B> 0^inf under an explicit map F on four kinds of tape (the reset S(x), the doubling round P(k, m), and two leftover shapes Q(u, n), T(u, v)) reaches a doubling round P(k, 0) that finds no 1s at all (halts_iff_H, lean/Map.lean). F is written as a Lean function and every one of its cases is a proved rule of the machine. The orbit does not halt in its first 107 nodes (Lean, compiled evaluation; 105 by the kernel) and, iterated in C, in its first 108 returns to S (X up to 1.5·1010); our own runs stop there.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 6,935 cells have been visited and 6,366 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.359). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.313).

claims.title: The doubling zig-zag and the sweeps
claims.text: One round of the zig-zag that doubles a block of pairs 10 while eating a block of 1s: L (10)^(j+1) (1111)^i F> 1 0 1^(m+2) R becomes L (10)^j 1^(4i+4) F> 1 0 1^m R in 8i+6 steps, for all i, j, m and any tapes L, R; and the four runs of the sweeps (E left over 1s; B, C, A right over pairs). Generated by py/rules.py.

claims.title: The doubling phase of a return, for every X
claims.text: Write S(X) for 0^inf 1^X 1110 B> 0^inf and P(k, m) for 0^inf F> 0 0 (10)^k 1^m R. Lean proves: the blank tape is in S(13) after 110 steps; S(X) reaches P(3, X) for X ≥ 6; for k ≥ 2 and m ≥ 2k + 3, P(k, m) reaches P(2k + 3, m − 2k − 3) (one doubling round: one pair becomes the wall block, k − 1 zig-zag rounds by induction, then the 1s are turned back into 2k + 3 pairs); and in closed form, if 12·2t ≤ X + 3t + 12 then S(X) reaches P(6·2t − 3, X + 3t + 12 − 12·2t). So the doubling phase ends, and the overflow starts, at the first t with 24·2t > X + 3t + 15: these are the doubling thresholds where f changes regime.

claims.title: The direct simulation agrees with the map
claims.text: c/reset_map.c starts the machine from S(X) = 0^inf 1^X 1110 B> 0^inf and runs it to the next configuration of the same shape. For all 1,281 values 6 ≤ X ≤ 1,300 that return or halt within 2·107 steps, the result is the one the Lean map F gives (the rest are the non-returning points below). This is a cross-check only: the map is a theorem (next claims).

claims.title: The overflow, for every size
claims.text: When the ones run out in the middle of a doubling round the tape is O(p, i, r) = 0^inf 1^6 0 (10)^p (1111)^i F> 1 0 1^r 0 1 0^inf (p pairs left, i zigs done, r < 2 ones left). Proved for all p, i: O(2q+1, i, 0) → P(2q+6, 4i+2); O(2q+1, i, 1) → T(q, 2i+3); O(2q+2, i, 0) → Q(q+1, 4i+7); O(2q+2, i, 1) → S(4q+4i+17); O(0, i, 0) → S(4i+7); O(0, i, 1) → S(4i+13). With Q(u, n) = 0^inf F> 0 0 (10)^3 (1110)^u 1^n 0 1 0^inf and T(u, v) = 0^inf F> 0 0 (10)^3 (1110)^u 1111 0 (10)^v 0 1 0^inf: Q(u+1, c+9) → P(2u+11, c), Q(u+1, 1) → S(4u+17), Q(u+1, 3) → Q(1, 4u+11), Q(u+1, 5) → P(6, 4u+10), Q(u+1, 7) → S(4u+19), T(u, v+1) → Q(1, 4u+2v+11); and the rounds that run out at once: P(k, 0) halts, P(k, 1) → S(2k+7) or Q(k/2, 3), P(k, 2) → T((k−1)/2, 1) or S(2k+9) (k odd or even). Each is one symbolic run (generated by py/overflow.py), restated on the named shapes in lean/Map.lean.

claims.title: Halts iff the orbit of S(13) reaches a round with no ones
claims.text: The nodes s x = S(x+6), p a m = P(a+3, m), q u c = Q(u+1, 2c+1), t u v = T(u, v+1) and the map F on them are Lean definitions; F_sem proves that every value of F is where the machine goes (in at least one step), and that F = none only where the machine halts. Hence: the machine halts from blank tape iff the orbit of s 7 (= S(13), reached at step 110) under F reaches none (halts_iff), iff it reaches a node p a 0, a doubling round 0^inf F> 0 0 (10)^(a+3) 0 1 0^inf (halts_iff_H). Only the standard axioms (propext, Quot.sound, Classical.choice).

claims.title: No halt in the first 100,000 nodes of the orbit
claims.text: orbitFrom (.s 7) 100000 evaluated by Lean's kernel is not none: the first 100,000 nodes (about 3,900 returns to S, up to S(407,853)) do not halt.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> nodes of the orbit
claims.text: The same evaluation for 10<sup>7</sup> nodes (about 299,000 returns, up to S(34,793,745)), by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>8</sup> returns
claims.text: c/orbit.c iterates the same map F (a transcription of the Lean definition, 64-bit counts): 108 returns to S (4.6·109 nodes, 6 seconds), X reaches 15,198,325,533, no node p a 0. Long stretches climb by exactly +100 per return; between some returns the orbit makes long excursions through P, Q and T nodes (up to 6.4·108 nodes) before coming back to S.

claims.title: f has halting and non-returning points
claims.text: For 6 ≤ X ≤ 1,300 the map F (and the direct simulation) halts before the next return exactly for X = 9, 30, 68, 75, 168, 295, 357, 738 (also 3,010 and 3,036), and never returns (an excursion through P, Q, T nodes that grows for ever, e.g. from S(41): Q(1, 71) → P(11, 62) → … → Q(3, 87) → … → Q(5, 103), the counts climbing by fixed amounts) for X = 41, 52, 63, 132, 273, 558, 1131 (and a few later values with long excursions). The halting points roughly double: 9, 30, 75, 168, 357, 738.

claims.title: Why the map looks Collatz-like
claims.text: Inside one return the zig-zag doubles a block of pairs, k → 2k + 3 from 3 (3, 9, 21, 45, 93, ...), until it runs out of 1s; the parity of the pairs left and of the 1s left then picks one of six overflow cases, some of which start a new, smaller doubling chain from a block of units 1110. So the next X depends on X modulo small powers of 2 and on where X lies between doubling thresholds: constant increments for long stretches (+40, +96, +100, ...), irregular jumps at thresholds. Each threshold is a fresh chance to land on a halting round.

claims.title: Reported: it halts (external Rocq proof, not compiled by us)
claims.text: busycoq pull request 60 (Yeyito) proves halts tm c0 in Rocq: the orbit of its map from blank tape reaches the halting case at a = 28·285 − 6 = 1083197534374707740536733690. It relies on 313 jobs evaluated by compiled code (275 core-hours). We have read it but not compiled it, so it is listed here as a report, not as a result of this repository.

claims.title: The external map and our Lean map agree
claims.text: Their state A(a, b) is our round P((a−6)/2, b). Their first 2,000,000 map steps appear, in order, among the first 2,181,564 nodes of our orbit, and from the round the external proof ends in, (22, 56·2<sup>85</sup> − 286), both maps reach the halt (85 steps there, 86 nodes here). The stretch in between is not checked by us.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Reported to halt by an external proof we have not compiled (see above). Within this repository it is still open: our orbit runs stop at 10<sup>8</sup> returns, far short of the reported halt.

check: python3 holdouts/1RB0LF_1RC1RA_0RD0RB_1LE---_0LA1LE_1RD1LA/py/overflow.py > lean/Overflow.lean   # regenerates the overflow rules

explainer.lede: Probably yes, after about 10<sup>55</sup> steps: an outside proof in Rocq says so, and we have not compiled it yet. Started on a blank tape this machine keeps coming back to a tape that is one block of 1s, and the length of that block is all that matters. It is a Lean theorem that the machine halts exactly when an explicit map, iterated from 13, reaches a doubling round with no 1s left; the outside proof follows the same map all the way to such a round. This page runs the real machine in your browser and explains the map.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 6,935 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).
Lean: halting is exactly a question about the orbit of S(13) under an explicit map.
The map iterated in C: no halt, X up to 1.5·10<sup>10</sup>.

sections.heading: One number on the tape
html: Most of the time the tape is almost featureless: a single block of 1s. Stop the simulator whenever the head, in state B, steps onto a new cell at the right end, and quite often the whole tape reads
0^inf 1^X 1 1 1 0 B> 0^inf   (call it S(X))

The first time is at step 110, with X = 13. Then come X = 29 (step 365), 45 (step 980), 137, 185, 217, 249, 345, ... Everything the machine does between two such moments depends only on X, so the whole run is the orbit of 13 under one map, X → f(X). In the first 2·109 steps the orbit has 161 points and has reached X = 9,265.

sections.heading: Doubling by zig-zag
html: Inside one return the head builds, at the left end of the block of 1s, a block of pairs 10, and then doubles it again and again. One round of the zig-zag takes one pair off the left block, crosses the block of 1s it has built, eats two 1s on the right and comes back:
(proved in Lean for all i, j, m). At the left end a pass then turns the 1s back into pairs. Watch the left end and the counts go
(a = 10): k → 2k + 3. When the doubled block no longer fits in the 1s, the round stops in the middle: that is the overflow, described in the next section.

In Lean this is a theorem for every X (S_rounds): after t rounds the tape is F> 0 0 (10)^(6·2t − 3) 1^(X + 3t + 12 − 12·2t) 0 1, as long as 12·2t ≤ X + 3t + 12. So the doubling stops at the first t with 24·2t > X + 3t + 15. For X = 137 that is t = 3 (block 45, 62 ones left); for X = 549, t = 5 (block 189, 192 ones left).

sections.heading: The whole map
html: When a round runs out of 1s the tape is
0^inf 1^6 0 (10)^p (1111)^i F> 1 0 1^r 0 1 0^inf   O(p, i, r)

with p pairs still to move, i zigs done and r = 0 or 1 ones left. What happens next depends only on the parities: the leftover pairs are swept back to the left end, two at a time; each pair of pairs becomes one unit 1110, an odd pair left over becomes a short block of pairs. The result is one of four shapes, all with the head at the left end in state F (or the reset S):

(Q only ever occurs with n odd, and T with v ≥ 1.) Example, X = 137: S(137) → P(3, 137) → P(9, 128) → P(21, 107) → P(45, 62); 62 ones are not enough for 93, so after 29 zigs O(15, 29, 1) → T(7, 61) → Q(1, 159) → P(11, 150) → P(25, 125) → P(53, 72) → O(18, 34, 1) → S(185).

Some starting values never come back to S: from S(41) the run goes Q(1, 71) → P(11, 62) → P(25, 37) → P(12, 70) → P(27, 43) → Q(3, 87) → … → Q(5, 103) → …, the same loop with counts that grow by fixed amounts, for ever. Others halt: S(X) reaches a round P(k, 0) for X = 9, 30, 68, 75, 168, 295, 357, 738, …

sections.heading: What halting would take
html: It is a Lean theorem (halts_iff_H) that the machine halts from blank tape exactly when the orbit of S(13) under these rules reaches a round P(k, 0): a doubling round that starts with no 1s at all. Everything else about the run is in the table above. So the open question is a question about one explicit map on four kinds of numbers, and nothing more.

The orbit 13, 29, 45, 137, 185, 217, 249, 345, 409, … has been followed for 108 returns to S (X up to 1.5·1010) without reaching P(k, 0); the first 107 nodes are also checked inside Lean. Proving that it never halts would mean proving that this orbit avoids a sparse but infinite set of bad values for ever. Every doubling threshold the orbit crosses is a new, irregular chance to hit one, which is what makes this a Collatz-like problem.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.359). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.313).
After 109 steps the tape spans 6,935 cells (4,354 left of the start, 1,219 right), with a density of 1s of 0.918.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: Reported to halt after about 10^55 steps by an external Rocq proof (busycoq PR 60, not compiled by us); our Lean theorem reduces halting to the same map (the orbit of S(13) reaching a doubling round with no 1s left), and the two maps agree where we could check.
